Thank you, Mr. President. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the African members of the Executive Board. We thank the agencies for the additional information and analysis provided. The group reiterates its position that the UNAT process should be guided by greater coherence, efficiency, effectiveness and accountability while preserving the mandates and capacities entrusted to the UN by Member States. We welcome the efforts to identify practical opportunities for reducing duplication, improving coordination and making better use of available resources. At the same time, UNAT should not be viewed as an exercise in reducing structures or costs. The fundamental question is whether the reforms pursued will ultimately lead to better results at country level. On the proposed merger between UNDP and UNOPS, the group welcomes the preparation of the terms of reference and supports proceeding with an independent assessment. Given the significance of the decision before Member States, the independence and credibility of this assessment are essential. The assessment should not presume that merger is a preferred outcome, it should objectively examine different merger configurations as well as, um, credible alternatives and clearly demonstrate their respective costs, benefits, risks and implications. For programme countries, particular attention must be given to the implications for country-level delivery, including whether the proposed arrangements would strengthen implementation capacity, preserve mandate-specific expertise, and improve responsiveness to national priorities. We therefore support meaningful engagement of programme countries throughout the assessment. The analysis should also comprehensively examine financial, operational, legal, and reputational risks, including scenarios where projected savings, revenues or efficiencies do not materialize. The board should have adequate visibility over the methodology and costs and progress of the assessment while safeguarding its independence. Mr. President, the discussion on UNFPA and UN Women provides an opportunity to consider whether greater efficiency and coherence can be achieved through common governance and closer institutional alignment without immediately undertaking a full structural merger. The analysis provided identifies genuine complementarities between the two agencies while also recognizing the costs, transition requirements, and risks associated with the merger. Importantly, it identifies alternative pathways for achieving greater coherence and efficiency, which could be pursued progressively while preserving their distinct mandates. The group sees merit in exploring ways to strengthen coordination between the executive boards of UNFPA and UN Women with a view to enhancing coherence, complementarity and efficiency while respecting their respective mandates and governance arrangements. Such an arrangement could strengthen strategic oversight, reduce duplication in governance and reporting and provide a more systematic platform for identifying efficiencies and joint results while allowing both organizations retain their distinct mandates, technical expertise and operational responsibilities. It could provide a practical middle ground, greater institutional coherence without immediately incurring the full transition costs and operational risks associated with a merger. However, this should not simply create another layer of bureaucracy. And any arrangement should have clear responsibilities, measurable objectives, and a mechanism for reviewing whether it is producing the intended efficiencies and improvements in delivery and impact. Mr. President, the group believes that the UNAT process should be sequenced, evidence-based, and results-oriented. We should move ahead where there is already a clear business case for greater collaboration. measure the results and savings, address implementation risks, and use evidence to inform decisions on deeper structural reforms. More importantly, efficiency gains should not come at the expense of mandate protection, specialized expertise, or continuity of country-level delivery. We reiterate that the objective and outcome should be a United Nations that is less fragmented, more coherent, financially sustainable, and accountable while remaining fully capable of delivering the mandates entrusted to it by Member States. That, in our view, should be the measure of success of UNAT. I thank you.

I thank Zambia for the statement delivered on behalf of the African Group. I have on the list Nepal on behalf of the Group of LDCs, Germany on behalf of Group of States, Uruguay on behalf of G77 and China. I give the floor to Nepal on behalf of the LDC Group.

Thank you, Mr. President. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Group of Least Developed Countries. The group appreciates the updates on the UNAD initiative and commends the efforts of the Secretary-General to ensure that the United Nations remains more efficient, accountable, and fit for purpose at a critical time of intensifying global challenges and acute financial pressures. The LDC Group supports the ongoing efforts to improve coordination, reduce fragmentation, strengthen accountability, and maximize the impact of every dollar invested in sustainable development. Mr. President, the Group would like to highlight three priorities. First, we reiterate that any UN reform process, including under the UNAD initiative, must remain firmly member-state led, transparent, inclusive, and evidence-based, fully respecting diversity of mandates, their context, and governance arrangements. We stress the importance of safeguarding mandates of particular relevance to LDCs, including those related to development financing, climate resilience, capacity building, sustainable graduation, and smooth transition. These commitments are fundamental to ensuring sustainable development pathways for our countries and should emerge stronger from the reform process. Second, the LDCs, home to nearly 1.2 billion people, continue to face persistent structural vulnerabilities, including climate shocks, financing constraints, food insecurity, infrastructure and capacity gaps, and growing debt burdens. They are struggling quite hard to stay on track in achieving the SDGs. We therefore call for reforms that reinforce rather than weaken the development pillar of the United Nations. For LDCs, the success of the UNAD reform initiative will be measured not by number of organizational changes undertaken, but by whether it extends support to program countries and accelerates tangible progress towards the sustainable development goals. We underscore that country level delivery must remain the central consideration throughout the reform process. Transition efforts should not divert resources, management attention or operational capacity away from support from for program countries. Ongoing country programs, cooperation frameworks, and nationally won development priorities must remain protected. Third, regarding discussions on potential structural reforms, including the proposed merger between UNDP and UNOPS, UNFPA and UN Women, we welcome the analytical work undertaken thus far. We note the preliminary assessments finding that these UN entities are distinct at complementary organizations with different mandates, funding models, and comparative advantages. We also recognize that the key challenge is not simply reducing duplication, but preserving the strengths of these institutions while improving coherence and effectiveness. From the perspective of the LDCs, the findings of the assessment reinforce a basic principle. Any reform must first and foremost stand on delivery for countries on the ground. We are encouraged that the assessment recognized the importance of preserving country presence long-standing partnership, trusted government relationships, and continuity of operations, which are among the most valued assets of the United Nations development system. Hence, the LDC Group strongly believes that any future decision on structural changes should be guided by clear evidence demonstrating that reforms will strengthen support to program countries, preserve national ownership and country-driven programming, protect development expertise and enhance implementation capacity, Deliver measurable results for those furthest behind and maintain continuity of delivery during any transition period. In closing, Mr. President, the LDC group remains committed to engaging constructively in the UNAT discussions to revitalize the LDCs. revitalize the United Nations that can deliver on the promises of its charter and respond to complex challenges of the 21st century. I thank you.
I thank Nepal for the statement on behalf of the LDC group. I give the floor to Germany, who will be speaking on behalf of group of states, please.

Mr. President, distinguished members of the executive board, excellencies, I have the honor to deliver the statement on behalf of a group of countries Australia, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Georgia, Iceland, Ireland, Japan, Kingdom of the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Malta, Monaco, New Zealand, Norway, Republic of Korea, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, United Kingdom, the European Union as a donor, and my own country, Germany. We reiterate our full support for the UN AT initiative. In accordance with the GCPR, we support greater coherence, complementarity and impact across the UN development system in line with countries priorities, while emphasizing that reforms must remain anchored in mandates and normative roles agreed by member states and translate into tangible improvements at country level. As stressed by the Secretary General, Member States are vital in crafting key outcomes of UNAT. To fulfill this role effectively, we need timely, robust and evidence-based information as well as inclusive and transparent opportunities for engagement across boards. With regard to UNFPA and UN Women, we welcome ongoing efforts to explore options for closer cooperation, greater alignment, institutional coherence, and organizational and operational improvements. The preservation, visibility, and full implementation of both organizations' unique and distinct mandates must remain a guiding principle for reform and are prerequisites for effective delivery. Any reform thus should be assessed not only in terms of efficiency, but also in terms of its impact on effective delivery for women, girls, young people, and communities in vulnerable situations. This is particularly important in the current global context marked by a growing pushback against gender equality, women's empowerment, SRHR, population dynamics and the principle of leaving no one behind. We therefore encourage UNFPA and UN Women to continue to strive for greater alignment, coordination and efficiency in a transparent manner. We remain open to considering options where evidence demonstrates clear added value, feasibility, cost effectiveness and a positive impact on delivery, as long as mandates and critical normative roles are protected. This safeguard is of paramount importance to us and must not be compromised at any stage of the process. With regard to UNDP and UNOPS, we appreciate the collaboration between the two entities on the joint development of a draft terms of reference. for the independent validation of the merger assessment. This process should provide a sound basis for Member States to consider a way forward in line with Decision 2026/16, including possible structural options such as a full merger of both organisations, while also identifying opportunities and alternatives for closer cooperation, greater efficiency and strengthened country-level Delivery. More broadly, these discussions should not be viewed in isolation. Other UNAD work packages, including, and we have heard it, UN country team reconfiguration, the regional reset, expertise on demand, and financing arrangements will also be essential to strengthen the impact, effectiveness, coherence, transparency, and accountability of the UN development system. We therefore call on all organizations concerned to engage fully and constructively in taking these reforms forward. We remain committed to engaging constructively across regions and across boards to shape a coherent evidence-based and member state-led way forward on UNAT, one that advances meaningful reform while preserving distinct mandates. normative work and strengths of each entity, leading to improved results for the people and communities they serve. I thank you.

I thank Germany for the statement delivered on behalf of a group of countries before giving the floor to Uruguay on behalf of a group of G77 and China. Thank you. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the G77 and China. The Group of 77 and China welcomes this interactive dialogue and wishes to reiterate the general support to the UNAD initiative and its overarching objective of achieving a paradigm shift in how the UN system organizes its work in order to deliver greater impact on the ground. With regard to the proposal to merge UNDP and UNOPS, the Group of 77 and China takes note of the terms of reference for independent assessment of a potential merger between UNDP and UNOPS, jointly developed by UNDP and UNOPS in line with the mandate set out in Executive Board decision 2026/16, engagement with the UNAT initiative, adopted at its annual session last June. The group values the terms of reference explicit recognition of the importance of ensuring geographic diversity in the composition of the assessment team should member states decide to endorse the terms of reference and proceed with the independent assessment. However, the role of member states, particularly poor and countries could be more explicitly reflected in the terms of reference and most importantly in the conduct of the assessment. Regular, inclusive and representative consultations with Member States would help ensure that the process is sufficiently transparent and that the findings and recommendations of the final assessment enjoy broad-based legitimacy. Mr. Chair, at a time of growing financial constraints and increasing development needs, and taking into account the numerous questions and concerns raised by member states across all regional groups regarding the proposed mergers, the Group of 77 and China believes that the necessary conditions are not in place to approve structural mergers that would entail a prolonged process of institutional restructuring. Therefore, the Group of 77 and China is of the view that Member States decision making processes on structural merger options that involve significant legal, operational, financial, and delivery risks, as well as direct impact at the operational level for program countries, should not be rushed during the current year. Instead, Attention should be directed towards country level delivery, including to accelerate progress in the implementation of national development priorities and the implementation of the SDGs. Therefore, the group welcomes the provision in the proposed timeline of the terms of reference that the final report will not be available before the 2027 annual session, as well as the commitment to provide the executive board with regular progress reports. The group considers that the Board should seek to agree on a pragmatic, concise and consensual UNHCR decision focused on advancing non-structural alternatives to the proposed mergers through enhanced coordination. This could include options identified in the joint UNDP/UNOPS report, such as combining selected operational functions to reduce administrative duplication and improve efficiency, as well as exploring potential joint ventures. Such arrangements could serve as an initial phase or as pilot initiatives enabling Member States to assess their impact and potential efficiency gains before considering whether more structural measures may be warranted in the future. In this regard, the proposed terms of reference for the independent assessment, if endorsed, adequately provide for the independent assessment to consider a range of possible merger modalities, as well as alternatives to a merger. Mr. Chair, to conclude, let me reassure you that the Group of 77 and China is aligned with the vision and ambition of the UNAT initiative and looks forward to working with all member states to contribute to reforms that improve efficiency and coordination while strengthening support to program countries. I thank you.

The reform should preserve the core functions and comparative advantages of each entity ensure the full retention of their existing mandates. This will help enhance their delivery capacity on the ground, strengthen to industry and coordination synergy, and better support the implementation of the 2030 agenda by the global south. We welcome the analysis submitted by UNFPA and UN Women on their reform, including the proposed merger and alternative options, and encourage the two entities to further engage with Member States so as to reach consensus. Third, reform must consolidate broad consensus among member states. Institutional reform bears on the long-term development of the UN development system. The reform should be transparent in the process, inclusive in participation, ensuring that the concerns and questions of all parties receive adequate responses. The UN aid reform provides an important opportunity for the UNDS to enhance its quality, effectiveness and efficiency, the development entities should seize the opportunity of the reform to optimize business processes, reduce administrative costs and orient entity setup and resource allocation more towards the country level. China is ready to continue to participate constructively in relevant discussions, work together with the broader membership to advance the relevant reform in a prudent and steady manner, and lay a solid foundation for the UN's development pillar. Thank you, President.

Denmark remains firmly committed to the UN and effective multilateralism. And this is not least signified by our 0.7 commitment and substantial core contributions to select UN funds and programs. In an increasingly challenging global context.

I thank Sweden for the statement. I give the floor now to the United Kingdom. And then we have the United States. We have Cuba, India, Norway, Japan, Armenia. I'll revise the list of speakers as we see that going. United Kingdom, please, you have the floor.

Thank you, Administrator, Executive Directors, Mr. President. The United Kingdom reiterates its strong commitment to the Secretary-General's UNAT reform agenda. I will make three points. First, delivery. The 2018 reform of the UN development system achieved much, however, important elements remain unfinished. We expect UN leadership to fully deliver this agenda. Key priorities include reconfiguring UN country teams and ensuring all UN development system work adheres to cooperation frameworks. Delivery must be improved through system-wide shared services, common enablers, notably technology and data. By consolidating and modernizing back office functions, the UN can build a leaner, more effective and resilient operational backbone. To support these efforts, it's crucial to empower resident coordinators and to lead one UN teams. Second, mandates. Institutional change must not undermine mandates entrusted to UN entities by member states. On the proposed UNFPA UN Women merger, there is not sufficient evidence for the UK to support a merger at this time, nor assurance that mandates will be protected. We have stood in union with other member states in calling for the preservation of distinct SRHR and gender equality mandates and are supportive of the aforementioned work packages. On UNDP and UNOPS, we appreciate the joint terms of reference and the independent assessment of the merger proposal and urge momentum in assessing reform proposals and continued collaborative working. Member States must have adequate opportunity to review and influence merger proposals, minimising disruption to ongoing operations, mitigating risks and protecting accountability mechanisms, particularly in fragile contexts. Third, evidence. Any merger decisions should be informed by strong evidence and full transparency regarding the costs of transition, the scale of efficiencies, the implications for future funding. We expect alternative approaches to be rigorously explored where they may deliver comparable benefits at lower cost and fewer associated risks. In conclusion, the UK supports UNAT and encourages UN leadership to fully implement the work packages and deliver a stronger UN able to deliver greater impact. I thank you.
I thank the United Kingdom for the statement. I give the floor now to the United States.

Good to see you, Cornell. Hi, Alexander. Hi, George. How are you guys? Look at that. Got some people to chuckle. Thank you for being here. The United States prioritizes reform of the United Nations system, including through UNAD, so that it remains fit for purpose for the next 80 years and beyond. Building on historic cost reductions and efficiency gains last year, we welcome bold changes that bring agencies back to core mandates, eliminate duplication, and improve return on member state investment. However, while some areas of work under UNAD have offered practical improvements, today we share our serious reservations regarding the return on investment of both this independent assessment and the proposed merger overall. We are being asked to consider committing increasingly scarce resources to a costly year-long consultancy simply to reconcile divergent data for a merger Member States did not propose and for which no rationale has been given. I feel compelled also to go off script here for a second and say that I think we all are aware of an agency within the UN family that has found a way to do a consultancy, albeit for a smaller project, gratis. They put an RFP out, they got three or four global consultancies to bid, and that work is being done as part of a corporate social responsibility at no cost. So a one and a half to two million dollar consultancy for a year is very different than a gratis one. And we would encourage for all the UN to be looking at that kind of model going forward. This comes alongside estimated merger transition costs reaching $250 million or more. In an era of shrinking budgets, every dollar spent on external consulting and administrative restructuring is a dollar diverted from direct field delivery. The business case remains speculative. with projected savings likely to be swallowed by transition friction, legal complexities, and operational disruption, with steady-state operation not anticipated until 2030. We do not believe this exercise offers a genuine return for Member States. Instead, we risk funding a costly bureaucratic process that yields minimal real-world benefit for the people we serve. Furthermore, we must express our disappointment at the inability of the agencies to collaboratively answer questions this board has asked. UN agencies capable of rebuilding economies, legislative and governance structures, and entire cities should be able to conduct objective analysis when requested by member states without seeking recourse to expensive private third parties. In turn, we are pleased to see you both come together with a common sense way forward. While always willing to consider concrete proposals and work with member states and secretariats to drive reform, we cannot support the terms of reference or a board decision for a costly and drawn out merger that the member states did not propose. I thank you.
I thank the United States for the statement. I give the floor to Cuba to be followed by India, Norway, Japan, and Armenia. Cuba, please.
